_comment: The ten-layer map. 'mode' is simulated, partial or discussed. 'engineVariables' are ids the engine actually computes; 'notSimulated' is what this layer teaches that the engine deliberately leaves out (spec 12).

layers.title: Demographics and geography
layers.plain: How many people there are, how old they are, where they live, and what the land gives them. This layer changes over decades, and it sets the limits of what everything above it can do.
layers.analogy: A village. If most people are over seventy there are fewer builders and more people needing care. If it sits on a river with good soil it can feed itself. If it sits in a desert with no port, trade is hard however clever the villagers are.
layers.discuss: Japan has been ageing for decades. The United States has had more immigration and a younger profile. Which businesses would you expect to do better in each place over twenty years?

layers.title: Energy and natural resources
layers.plain: Almost everything in the physical economy burns, moves or stores energy. Energy is not one sector among many. It is an input to transport, manufacturing, food, heating and computing alike, so when it gets expensive, costs rise nearly everywhere.
layers.analogy: If petrol doubles overnight, the delivery van, the farm tractor, the plastic in the packaging and the heating bill all get dearer. The bakery has a worse month even though nobody's taste in bread changed.
layers.watch: Oil and gas prices, copper, food prices.
layers.discuss: Which parts of the economy might benefit from a higher oil price, and which would suffer?
layers.engineNote: You control this layer directly. The energy supply shock is the model's second input, and it lands in the same quarter you set it.

layers.title: Production and supply chains
layers.plain: Resources become products and services here: factories, farms, building sites, mines, software and shipping. Productivity lives in this layer. If the same worker produces more, growth and profits can rise without as much inflation.
layers.analogy: A phone is not made in one place. Minerals are mined, chips are fabricated, screens are made, software is written, the device is assembled, then it ships. If one link snaps, the whole chain slows.
layers.watch: Industrial production, factory orders, chip output.
layers.discuss: If a country cannot make advanced semiconductors, which later layers become harder for it?

layers.title: International trade
layers.plain: Countries swap what they are good at making. Trade is the plumbing between national production systems. When governments tax imports, block sales, or when ships cannot move, prices and availability change in the shops.
layers.analogy: Your local supermarket is the last aisle of a global warehouse. If the warehouse is delayed, the shelf looks empty or the price jumps, even though the shop did nothing wrong.
layers.watch: Container rates, trade balances, tariff announcements.
layers.discuss: Why do wars and export controls turn up in an economics class rather than only a politics one?

layers.title: Labour, income and consumption
layers.plain: Production pays people, people spend, and that spending is someone else's revenue. Household spending is a large share of activity in most rich economies, which is why the consumer appears in every forecast.
layers.analogy: A town with a busy factory pays good wages. The cafe opposite is full, so it hires another cook. The cook rents a flat. The landlord spends the rent at the hardware shop. One payroll becomes many receipts.
layers.discuss: If wages rise more slowly than prices, is the economy growing or shrinking for the people in it?
layers.engineNote: Growth and inflation are simulated here. Jobs and wages are not: the model speaks about employment rather than computing it.

layers.title: Savings, credit and investment
layers.plain: Income that is not spent becomes savings, and the financial system's job is to send those savings to people who want to invest. Bonds, loans and shares are not magic tickets. They are pipes. When the pipes clog, investment falls and future growth is weaker.
layers.analogy: You skip takeaways for a year and put the money in the bank. The bank lends it to a builder putting up flats. Your leftover sandwiches helped create housing.
layers.watch: Lending standards, loan growth, credit spreads.
layers.discuss: Why is the stock market not the same thing as the economy?
layers.engineNote: This is the layer the whole lesson turns on. Credit carries a one-quarter lag, so a rate rise leaves it completely unmoved in the quarter of the decision.

layers.title: Central banks and interest rates
layers.plain: The most important short-term transmission mechanism. The interest rate is the price of money over time. Raise it and new mortgages, car loans and business loans get dearer, so people borrow and spend less, which cools demand and eventually inflation.
layers.analogy: A thermostat. Inflation running hot, turn the heating down. Economy frozen, turn it up. The thermostat does not cook dinner. It changes the room so that everything else happens differently.
layers.watch: The policy rate and what the bank says it will do next.
layers.discuss: If inflation is high because oil is scarce, will raising interest rates fix the oil shortage? What will it do instead?
layers.engineNote: You set the rate, or you hand the job to the rule and watch the bank react. Note there is no direct line from the rate to growth: it has to travel through credit, energy and wealth.

layers.title: The US dollar and government bonds
layers.plain: Close to the centre of the global financial system. Much of world trade and debt is priced in dollars even when neither side is American, and government bonds set the benchmark that everything else is valued against.
layers.analogy: Treasuries are the school's official measuring stick. If the stick itself gets dearer to use, every other project has to look more attractive to be worth doing. That is why a move in US yields can knock share prices in London and house prices in Sydney.
layers.watch: The ten-year yield and the dollar index.
layers.discuss: Say the inverse rule out loud until it is boring: yields up, bond prices down.
layers.engineNote: Both move in the same quarter as the shock. There is one long rate, not a curve.

layers.title: Asset markets
layers.plain: Once growth expectations, inflation, rates and the dollar are in motion, they show up in prices. A share price is expected future profits divided by the return investors demand, so two quite different things can move it: the profits, or the discount rate.
layers.analogy: Good news for the economy is not always a good day for shares. If the good news makes people expect higher rates, valuations can fall even while profits rise.
layers.watch: Valuations against profits, not the index level alone.
layers.discuss: If the central bank surprises everyone with a big rise, what happens to equities, bonds, housing and gold, and why?
layers.engineNote: Equity is simulated and computed last in the quarter, so the shock quarter already contains the full financial hit. Property and gold are discussed only.

layers.title: The feedback loop
notSimulated: anything the model calls a breakpoint
layers.plain: The hierarchy is not a one-way staircase. Asset prices change wealth, wealth changes spending, spending changes profits and jobs and inflation, and inflation changes what the central bank does next.
layers.analogy: If house prices and share prices fall, households cut back even when their wages have not changed. Economists call it the wealth effect.
layers.watch: Whether a market move is starting to show up in spending.
layers.discuss: Trace an oil shock all the way round until it pushes the oil price back down.
layers.engineNote: One strand of this loop is simulated: the equity-to-growth link is the wealth effect, and it feeds market moves back into the real economy with a one-quarter lag. Confidence effects beyond that are discussed only.
